Two weeks ago, the Climate Aligned Finance Act (CAFA) was reintroduced into the Senate by Senator Rosa Galvez. Through a number of legislative proposals, CAFA seeks to limit both the risks that financial institutions pose to the climate, and the risks climate change poses to Canada's financial system.

CAFA was first introduced in March of 2022, where it was endorsed by 89 investment firms, academic organizations, and environmental groups, and heralded as one of the most ambitious pieces of climate legislation currently underway. At the Toronto Climate Observatory, we looked to CAFA to help inform the recommendations of our inaugural Bay St. Climate Report (linked below). CAFA has been similarly upheld by environmental organizations and sustainable finance experts, including Environmental Defence and Shift Action for Pension Wealth and Planet Health, as an amalgamation of leading thought on climate-aligned legislation in Canada.

This new version of CAFA includes most of the important sections from its first iteration, while changing some pieces that were holding it up under its first reading. In its current version, CAFA includes actions such as: 

📌 Mandating financial institutions to develop emissions reductions targets that align with climate commitments.

✅ Requiring financial institutions create climate transition plans detailing their plans to achieve these targets.

➡️ Directing federal regulators to create guidelines on transition risks and exposures for financial institutions.

🔎 Enforcing the disclosure of conflicts of interest, with regards to the fossil fuel industry, by any individual who sits on the board of a financial institution.

Our work at the Toronto Climate Observatory has shown that voluntary commitments from financial institutions are insufficient, further positioning this bill as a critical step in Canada's climate transition. As it moves forward through the legislative process, CAFA remains a benchmark piece of legislation in Canada, providing the structural rules and accountability necessary to align our financial system with climate action. 

For more information, read this summary from Environmental Defence Canada: https://lnkd.in/gY8Xx3S7 

Watch this interview with Senator Rosa Galvez: https://lnkd.in/esP78eyX 

Learn how this relates to the 2025 Federal Budget from Shift Action: https://lnkd.in/guMYwdiy 

Read our 2024 Bay St. Climate Report: https://lnkd.in/eYfsKJsC

📣 Workshop alert! Technologies: Data, tools, and infrastructures will bring to you an examination of the technical foundations that enable effective flood risk management in Southern Ontario.

🗓️ Tuesday, October 14, 2025
🕐 1 pm - 2.30 pm
👩‍💻 Open to all municipal and conservation authority staff from Southern Ontario
👥 Co-hosted by Toronto Climate Observatory & Climate Action Partnership
💌 Reach out to taneea@cs.toronto.edu for registration details

💡 What to expect:
Join us for an in-depth workshop to explore how the technologies behind our flood information systems shape who gets access to critical data — and who doesn't — from the nature of the data we collect, to the tools we use to analyze and communicate flood information. We'll examine how hydrometric networks, satellite monitoring, hydraulic modeling software, and sensor technologies work together to create flood information systems — and how these technical choices can either support or hinder equitable access to vital flood data.

🎙️ Special guest speaker:
Dr Rodrigo Costa, Assistant Professor, Systems Design Engineering, University of Waterloo

Dr Costa's research focuses on societal and environmental systems and examines how communities' physical, economic, and social systems interact to exacerbate disaster risk and further socioeconomic and racial inequalities. His goal is to inform targeted interventions to reduce disaster impacts, accelerate recovery, and ensure that all of society participates in the benefits.

Talk title: Repeated and localized flooding is an underestimated challenge for urban disaster risk management

Talk description: While large-scale disasters attract national and federal attention and assistance, localized flood events often don't qualify for external aid — despite being just as devastating for those impacted. Dr. Costa will present a methodology to evaluate long-term impacts of repeated, localized disasters, showing how a 20-year flood with no external assistance can lead to greater cumulative losses than a 100-year flood event.

🌍 Why it matters:
Together, we'll explore how today's flood data systems and modeling tools shape equity outcomes, and discuss how we might redesign data collection, processing, and dissemination systems to better serve all communities and support equitable flood risk management across Southern Ontario.

👥 Who should attend:
All municipal staff and conservation authority staff from Southern Ontario are welcome, particularly those working on flood risk management, infrastructure resilience, and climate adaptation in Southern Ontario.

📩 Interested in attending?
 Reach out to taneea@cs.toronto.edu for more details and registration.

🎙️ TCO Voices: Hear from Dylan Van Bramer, a new addition to the TCO! ✨ 
Dylan joins the Toronto Climate Observatory as both a new PhD student in the University of Toronto's Computer Science department and as a researcher eager to bridge computation and community. She reflected with us on what drew her to TCO, the questions inspiring her research, and what she most looks forward to this semester.

📖 How did your journey lead you to the University of Toronto for your doctoral studies?
I studied computer science as an undergraduate at Cornell, where I became drawn to research as a way to bridge technical rigor with questions that matter in the world. UofT felt like the perfect place to explore these intersections, especially with the opportunity for joint supervision from professors working across different dimensions of machine learning and human-computer interaction.

🍁 What drew you to the Toronto Climate Observatory?
The TCO is unique and distinctive in its hyperlocal orientation, grounding computational research in the realities of place and community – something we don't see very often in computer science departments. It's inspiring and exciting to witness traditionally inaccessible computational research being transformed into sites of consultation and co-creation with Toronto's communities. This place-based focus, and the TCO's mandate to reflect critically on ethics, systems, and forms of knowledge, is what really excites me about being part of this work.

💡 What research interests call out to you as you begin your PhD journey?
I'm interested in environmental data and how we can use it responsibly in modeling. I care a lot about the interpretability of models – people need to meaningfully understand what algorithms are doing if they're going to trust them, especially when those algorithms inform big decisions. I'm also curious about how environmental data is collected and used, and the biases that can shape those processes. Ultimately, I want to think about machine learning in a more conscious, thoughtful way, and bring together computational methods with community approaches to solve real problems.

👩‍💻 What are you most excited about this semester?
I'm really looking forward to getting to know everyone at the TCO and learning about the wide range of projects underway, from pure climate science to work immersed deeply within the community. That breadth is energizing, because it means I'll get to learn from many different methods and ways of thinking as I begin shaping my own research path. More than anything, I'm looking forward to the conversations, and being in dialogue with colleagues who are asking different, but complementary, questions about climate, computation, and community.

📣 Project Spotlight: Reimagining our relationship with water through the Toronto Water Atlas 

🌊 Over the last eight months, the Toronto Water Atlas (TWA) team, supported by the TCO, has been working to re-examine and understand our relationship with water - not simply as a natural resource or a problem to be managed, but as a life-giving source, and a connector of people and of communities. 

The Atlas is imaginative, interactive, and collaborative - a critical and artistic exploration of how water shapes the present and future of the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA), and the GTHA's relationship with its rivers, creeks, and waterways. The Atlas goes beyond maps of water systems and flood risks to ask bigger questions:
✅ How do we live with water rather than simply manage it?
✅ How do we navigate our relationship with water not merely as a resource, but as a shaper of ecosystems, cultures, and communities?
✅ How can water guide climate resilience, equity, and cultural connection?

Since January, the team has hosted:
📍 8 community workshops (Saturdays, 2 - 5 PM)
📍 14+ co-working sessions (Tuesdays, 6 - 9 PM)
…bringing together researchers, artists, technologists, and community members to collaborate on maps, stories, and speculative designs.

The team also recently showcased some of their maps at COMPASS 2025 - check out one of them here: https://lnkd.in/gVwSUXZ5 

🌐 Curious? Explore more on the TWA's (currently evolving!) website: https://lnkd.in/g6nxDe3U

📣 Get involved!
If you're working on an artistic, critical, or speculative mapping project around water in Toronto - or if you'd like to join the TWA workshops or co-working sessions - reach out at taneea@cs.toronto.edu

🎤 From July 22 - 25, University of Toronto hosted the 2025 iteration of the ACM, Association for Computing Machinery Conference on Computing and Sustainable Societies (COMPASS)! 🌱 

Some key highlights from the conference:

🌎 This year, COMPASS welcomed 221 attendees from 22 countries, 42 of whom were from 12 countries in the Global South. 

👩‍💻 An inspiring and diverse community of contributors from across borders and disciplines came together to make this conference a success: 36 members on the Organizing Committee, 89 dedicated reviewers, 16 incredible volunteers - plus 69 paper presentations across 17 sessions, 6 insightful panels, and so much more!

📍This year's theme - "computing in place" - was an exploration of interdisciplinary research on sustainability with a focus on how computing and moves toward sustainability are embedded in and shaped by specific local contexts. COMPASS welcomed work that critically examines how technology intersects with social, environmental, and economic systems, encouraging a deeper, situated perspective on how technological practices emerge as solutions, but also as contributors to the complexities they claim to address.

🎙️This year's conference featured two incredible keynote speakers - Renee Sieber, Associate Professor at McGill University, who spoke about participatory AI governance as a sustainability goal, and Pedro Reynolds-Cuéllar, Research Scientist at the Robotics and AI Institute, who explored why designing with place matters for technology development.

🌟 Watch this space for more highlights from COMPASS 2025!

📢 Impact Spotlight: TCO's Bay Street Climate Report spurs new City Council motion on addressing the financial industry's carbon footprint!
 
On March 26 and 27, 2025, the Toronto City Council, led by Councillor Paula Fletcher, and seconded by Dianne Saxe, adopted a motion to address the financial industry's carbon footprint. Influenced by the TCO's Bay Street Climate Report, which found that Bay Street financial institutions financed 1.44 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions in 2022, City Council adopted five actions to address this impact. 

Read about the motion here: https://lnkd.in/gB_v8qct

Check out the TCO's Bay Street Climate Report here: https://lnkd.in/gfWT5qEj

🚨 New Research Incoming @ TCO! 📚
We're excited to announce two new research grants that the TCO has recently been awarded! These grants will allow us to deepen our work at the intersection of flooding, equity, and infrastructure resilience in Southern Ontario and beyond:

🔷 Urban Challenge Grant – School of Cities, University of Toronto
 TCO has been awarded the 2025-26 Urban Challenge Grant from the University of Toronto's School of Cities, as part of its latest call focused on inequality, data, and democracy. Building on our past collaboration evaluating public flood data in the GTA, this project will develop a framework to assess the equity, quality, and usability of public flood information. Our goal is to identify priorities for improving flood information infrastructures and inform smarter, more equitable investments in these infrastructures across Southern Ontario. Read about all grant recipients here: https://lnkd.in/gZ8cEPHy

🔶 2025–2027 Joint EMHSeed & XSeed Grant – Faculty of Applied Science & Engineering (FASE)
TCO has also received funding from the Joint EMHSeed and XSeed Program at U of T, in collaboration with FASE and the Faculty of Arts & Science. This interdisciplinary initiative will launch a flood reconnaissance team to investigate how past and future flood events impact underserved communities and the built environment in the GTA. We'll co-develop data collection protocols with community partners, build initial tech infrastructure needed to conduct post-flood reconnaissance in select communities in the GTA, and study local and national flood events to generate actionable, community-informed insights.

Together, these projects advance our mission to:
 ✅ Improve flood resilience
 ✅ Build equitable data systems
 ✅ Support communities most impacted by climate risk

We're deeply grateful to our partners, collaborators, and funders for their support and shared commitment to advancing equitable climate solutions. Stay tuned as we share research milestones, community insights, and opportunities to get involved!

🔎 Event Recap: The Looming LNG Glut – Market Assessment & Risks

This week, the TCO co-hosted a webinar with Schulich Centre of Excellence in Responsible Business (COERB) and Trottier Family Foundation exploring the growing risks of a global LNG oversupply and what it means for markets, policymakers, and the energy transition.

💡 Key insights from Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA)'s Clark Williams-Derry:

📉 A glut is on the horizon
Between 2025 and 2029, global LNG export capacity is projected to grow by ~40%, led by massive buildouts in the U.S., Qatar, Canada, and beyond. Global supply is set to outstrip demand well into the 2030s, putting financial pressure on new LNG projects and heightening the risk of stranded assets.

🪫 Demand is projected to decline
Europe, Japan, and South Korea - together accounting for 50% of global LNG demand - are all on long-term paths to reduce gas use. Meanwhile, demand in developing economies like China, India, Pakistan, and Vietnam is constrained by affordability, energy security concerns, competition from renewables, and policy headwinds.

🌱 Climate risks are real
Prolonged oversupply could slow the energy transition by making fossil gas artificially competitive with renewables - especially in emerging markets.

💰 Investor implications
Falling spot prices and weaker margins raise tough questions: Who is exposed? Which projects are resilient? And how can investors distinguish between short-term gains and long-term risks?

This session highlighted the need for granular, realistic analysis when assessing new LNG infrastructure in a rapidly changing energy landscape. A big thank you to our speakers and co-hosts for this compelling, data-rich conversation!

In case you missed it, watch the webinar recording here: https://lnkd.in/gdrgrxYr

🎓 Last month, we officially wrapped up the Toronto Climate Summer School (TCSS) after six transformative weeks of learning! 

Hosted by the School of the Environment and the Toronto Climate Observatory, TCSS 2025 brought together an incredible cohort of undergraduate students, faculty, and community partners for an immersive experience exploring climate change through a uniquely local, justice-focused lens.

Over six weeks, students engaged in a full-time program that combined coursework, tutorials, workshops, and site visits in the first half, followed by dedicated, faculty-supervised research in the second half. The program culminated in a poster presentation session in mid-June, where students showcased the research they undertook during the summer school.

🎤 Here's what some of our students had to say:

Nicole Stochmal, Psychology and Environmental Science: "A key takeaway from this experience is that effective climate adaptation must be shaped by those most affected. Solutions are most impactful when grounded in experience rather than imposed through top-down policy frameworks. I also came to see research not just as a tool for analysis, but as a means of listening, building relationships, and advocating for more just and inclusive futures."

Chaewon Kang, Political Science and Environmental Studies: "I'm walking away with a lifelong community built through 6 weeks of intense collaboration and learning with my peers. Most of all, I now feel a stronger sense of readiness and confidence to apply what I've learned to bring about meaningful change and contribute to solving local challenges."

🌱 This year's TCSS demonstrated what's possible when rigorous academic training meets meaningful, community-engaged climate learning. A huge thank you to our faculty mentors, community partners, and inspiring student cohort for making TCSS 2025 such a success.

💡 Stay tuned for future opportunities!
